intro: You've searched for an appeal immigration advisor near you, so you're likely facing a refusal and wondering what to do next. The appeal process can feel confusing and deadlines are short, but a local adviser can help you understand your options. We introduce you to a suitable UK professional who will quote you directly.
need_heading: What people searching for an appeal immigration advisor usually need
need_lead: Most people in this situation need clear guidance on whether they can appeal and how to proceed.
needs: You've received a refusal letter and want to know if you have a right of appeal or if another route is available.
You need help understanding the appeal deadline and what steps to take before it passes.
You have new evidence that wasn't considered before and want to know if it can be used in an appeal.
You're unsure whether your case needs an appeal to the First-tier Tribunal, an administrative review or a judicial review.
You want to find a local adviser who is properly regulated and can represent you at a hearing.
context_heading: One key thing to understand about immigration appeals
context: Not every refusal comes with a right of appeal. The type of decision and your circumstances determine whether you can appeal to the First-tier Tribunal, request an administrative review or seek a judicial review. Deadlines are very short, so it's important to act quickly.

It is a criminal offence to give immigration advice in the UK unless you are qualified and regulated. Advisers must be registered with the Immigration Advice Authority (IAA, formerly the OISC) at the right level for your matter, or be a solicitor, barrister or chartered legal executive authorised by their own regulator. Always check the IAA's adviser finder or the SRA register before sharing documents or paying.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when you enquire
tell: The date on your refusal letter and the type of application you made.
Whether the refusal letter mentions a right of appeal or any other review options.
Any new evidence you have that wasn't available before the decision.
Your current immigration status and whether you have any upcoming deadlines.
The level of urgency, such as if your appeal deadline is approaching.
Your location and whether you need someone to represent you in person or can work remotely.
questions: Are you registered with the Immigration Advice Authority or are you a solicitor or barrister regulated by your own body?
What level of registration do you hold, and does it cover appeals and representation?
Do you think I have a right of appeal, and if so, what is the deadline?
What are the possible outcomes of an appeal in my situation?
Can new evidence be considered in my appeal, and how should I present it?
What are your fees and how will you keep me informed throughout the process?

faqs.q: Do I always have a right of appeal against an immigration refusal?
faqs.a: No, not every refusal carries a right of appeal. The refusal letter should state whether you can appeal, and if not, whether other options like administrative review or judicial review are available. An adviser can help you understand your specific case.

faqs.q: How quickly do I need to act after a refusal?
faqs.a: Deadlines for appeals and reviews are very short, often just days or a few weeks. It's important to seek advice as soon as possible so you don't miss the deadline.

faqs.q: Can I introduce new evidence in my appeal?
faqs.a: Fresh evidence may help your appeal, but there are rules about when and how it can be considered. An adviser can tell you what evidence is relevant and how to present it.

faqs.q: How do I check that an immigration adviser is properly regulated?
faqs.a: You can check the Immigration Advice Authority's adviser finder or the Solicitors Regulation Authority register. Always do this before sharing documents or paying any money.

extra_heading: Choosing a local appeals adviser and what to expect
extra: Searching for an appeal immigration advisor near you suggests you want someone you can meet face to face, perhaps because your case involves sensitive documents or you feel more comfortable discussing your refusal in person. When you contact local advisers, ask whether they offer appointments at their office or whether they can travel to you, and check that their registration covers appeals and representation at the First-tier Tribunal. It's also worth asking how they handle urgent deadlines if you instruct them at short notice.

At a first appointment, a regulated adviser will usually review your refusal letter and any supporting documents, explain whether you have a right of appeal or whether another route such as administrative review or judicial review applies, and outline the deadline you're working towards. They may also discuss what fresh evidence could strengthen your case and how to gather it. You should leave with a clear idea of your options and the likely next steps, along with an explanation of their fees.

When comparing advisers, don't be swayed by claims of being the best or cheapest. Instead, check that they are properly regulated for appeals work, ask about their experience with cases like yours, and make sure you understand what their quote covers. A good adviser will be transparent about fees and timelines, and will not pressure you into instructing them on the spot.

extra_faqs.q: Can I switch advisers if I've already started an appeal?
extra_faqs.a: Yes, you can change advisers, but it's important to do so quickly so the new adviser has time to review your case before any deadline. You should inform your current adviser and request your file, and check whether any fees are outstanding.

extra_faqs.q: What should I bring to my first appointment with an appeals adviser?
extra_faqs.a: Bring your refusal letter, any other correspondence from the Home Office, and any evidence you think is relevant, such as new documents that weren't considered before. It also helps to bring a note of your immigration history and any deadlines you're aware of.
